questions.stem: The small intestine is lined with millions of villi. Each villus is covered in microvilli. How does this arrangement maximise nutrient absorption?

options.text: It slows down the movement of food, giving more time for digestion
It massively increases the surface area for absorption, allowing more nutrients to be absorbed at once
It produces more enzymes for digestion
It creates a thicker barrier to protect the intestine

questions.explanation: Villi and microvilli together increase the surface area of the small intestine by approximately 600 times compared to a flat surface. This enormous surface area means that many more nutrient molecules can be absorbed simultaneously across the intestinal wall, making absorption extremely efficient.

questions.stem: Villi have a rich blood supply (dense capillary network). How does this help with absorption?

options.text: Blood provides enzymes to digest remaining food
Blood quickly carries absorbed nutrients away, maintaining a steep concentration gradient for diffusion
Blood heats the villi to increase enzyme activity
Blood provides oxygen for photosynthesis in the villi

questions.explanation: The constant blood flow through villus capillaries carries absorbed nutrients (glucose, amino acids) away from the intestinal wall quickly. This maintains a low concentration of these nutrients in the blood near the villi, keeping a steep concentration gradient between the gut lumen and the blood, which drives faster diffusion.

questions.stem: Glucose absorption in the small intestine occurs partly by diffusion and partly by active transport. Why is active transport necessary?

options.text: Diffusion is too slow for any glucose to be absorbed
Active transport ensures all glucose is absorbed, even when the concentration in the blood is already higher than in the gut
Active transport converts glucose into starch for storage
Glucose cannot diffuse through cell membranes

questions.explanation: Initially, when glucose concentration in the gut is high after a meal, glucose is absorbed by diffusion. But as concentrations equalise, diffusion slows. Active transport uses energy (ATP) to continue absorbing glucose against the concentration gradient, ensuring virtually all glucose is absorbed from food rather than being lost.

questions.stem: The epithelial cells lining the villi are only one cell thick. Why is this thin wall important for efficient absorption?

options.text: Thin walls produce more enzymes
A shorter diffusion distance means nutrients can cross more quickly from the gut lumen to the blood
Thin walls allow the villi to move and mix food
Thin walls prevent bacteria from entering the blood

questions.explanation: The rate of diffusion is inversely related to the distance the molecules must travel. A single layer of epithelial cells (about 0.01 mm thick) means nutrients have a very short diffusion pathway from the gut lumen to the blood capillaries, greatly increasing the speed of absorption.

questions.stem: A patient with coeliac disease has damaged villi that are much flatter than normal. Which of the following symptoms would you expect?

options.text: Increased nutrient absorption and weight gain
Weight loss, fatigue, and nutrient deficiencies due to reduced surface area for absorption
Increased appetite with no other symptoms
Improved digestion because enzymes work better on flat surfaces

questions.explanation: Flattened villi drastically reduce the surface area available for nutrient absorption. This means fewer nutrients from food are absorbed into the blood, leading to malnutrition despite eating normally. Symptoms include weight loss, fatigue (from reduced glucose and iron absorption), anaemia, and vitamin deficiencies.
